The morning light hit the windowsill differently today, and I found myself thinking about how we measure time in these tiny, unrepeatable increments. A shadow falls a particular way. A coffee cools to exactly the right temperature. We don't have clocks for these things, but our bodies know.

I've been reading about mycelial networks, how fungi connect trees in forests through threads too small to see, allowing a birch to send nutrients to a struggling oak. The "wood wide web," someone called it, and I keep returning to this image: all that hidden communication, all that quiet support happening in darkness beneath our feet. We walk through forests assuming individual trees, standing alone in their strength, when really they're holding hands underground.

It makes me wonder what networks exist that I fail to perceive. The way a mood passes through a household before anyone speaks. How a neighborhood shifts when one person starts tending their garden, then another, then suddenly there's a corridor of blooming things where before there was only lawn. We are always participating in systems larger than our intentions.

I want to be more like the oak receiving sugar from the birch—not too proud to accept, not too independent to need. There's a vulnerability in admitting you're kept alive by invisible threads, that your thriving depends on transfer you cannot control or even fully witness.

The coffee's cold now. The shadow has moved. Something is always ending, something always beginning, and we are threaded through it all, giving and receiving in ways we'll never map completely.
